The trees have made the most of this — each branch a careful ledge, holding its portion of white with the concentration of something that knows it is temporary and has decided to be thorough anyway. A door. Somewhere behind it, a radio beginning. The smell of something warm — coffee, or bread — that reaches the street and then dissolves, surprised by its own ambition. Then a figure: coat, scarf, the breath making its brief appearance and disappearing, a small autobiography of warmth written in cold air and immediately revised. The footsteps begin. The surface accepts them, each one a small negotiation — the street becoming, step by step, a place where morning is in progress, where the night's perfect arrangement is undone by the cheerful ordinary damage of someone simply needing to be somewhere. The lamp clicks off. The day has begun without asking.

**The Room** Everything is smaller. This is the first law of return — the ceiling has come down to meet you, the window that once framed the entire available world has settled into being just a window, the garden beyond it just a garden, modest and unmagical in the afternoon light. The wardrobe still has the mark where I measured my height in pencil, a stratigraph of former selves — here at seven, here at nine, the hopeful lurch between twelve and thirteen when I thought I might be tall, the plateau after that, the body's small betrayal. The wallpaper: those boats. I spent so many ceilinged hours captaining them silently through the elaborate weather of a childhood afternoon. They have not moved. They are not going anywhere. They never were. Under the bed, still: the particular dust of a room that has been waiting. A book I never finished. A torch with dead batteries from some urgency I can't remember but must have felt. I sit on the edge of the mattress and the springs say the same thing they always said — that specific complaint, unchanged, patient, the room's one form of greeting. Outside, the street goes on with its present-tense concerns. In here it is always the hour before something. Always the last summer. Always the version of me that is about to leave and does not know that leaving is the easy part.

**September's Edge** Something knows before you do. The light, perhaps — it hasn't changed exactly, but it has changed its mind about how long to stay, leaning now at an angle it didn't bother with in July, casting shadows that are longer than the afternoon deserves, autumn already practising its longer signature. Or the quality of the air — still warm, but a warmth that is making arrangements, that has checked the calendar and found something it didn't like. The trees are keeping their own counsel but you notice, if you're paying attention, the first small resignations, a leaf here, a yellowing there, the first tentative surrenders of a slow negotiation. You know it's the last one. Not because of the date — dates are someone else's agreement with time — but because the afternoon has that particular fullness, the way things have when they are ending and know it, a ripeness that is also a kind of goodbye. The children in the park do not know this. They are simply playing, which is perhaps the correct response. The ice cream van makes its usual argument and is believed. You sit with it a little longer than you need to. The drink in your hand. The unremarkable sky doing nothing more than being blue and being there and being, for this hour, entirely enough. Then the light shifts. A door, somewhere, closes. And summer, with no particular ceremony, lets go.

**Across the Street** Third floor, late afternoon, the window my accidental theatre — I wasn't looking for anything and found this: a man on the opposite pavement doing something with his keys. Not finding them — he has them — doing something else, something that has no name in the catalogue of ordinary gestures. Turning them, maybe. Considering them. Standing at the edge of going in and not, quite, going in. He doesn't know I'm here. This is the contract of windows — the watcher absolved by glass and distance and the simple fact that no one thinks to look up when they are standing with their keys at the edge of whatever this is. I construct him, as one does. A day that went sideways. News received and being processed in the only private space left — a pavement, a set of keys, a moment stolen from the seen world for something the seen world doesn't need to witness. Or nothing. Perhaps nothing. Perhaps he simply likes his keys. Perhaps I am the sentimental one, finding thresholds where there are only pavements, finding stories where there is only a man going home a little more slowly than usual. He goes in. The door closes. The street resumes its business, indifferent as streets always are to the small unwitnessed ceremonies taking place along them. I turn from the window. Somewhere a key turns in a lock and something opens, or doesn't, and no one sees either way.
